expected.name: Ulysses DeRosa
expected.description: Ulysses DeRosa was a Quaker conscientious objector imprisoned during World War I. Court-martialed for refusing military service, he was held at Fort Leavenworth. Sentenced to 25 years. (Documented in the Swarthmore College Peace Collection's World War I Conscientious Objectors database.) Archival note: born in Italy in 1892; emigrated to America in 1905; joined the Quakers in 1916; taken to Ft. Slocum for a few days, where he refused to sign induction papers; an absolutist CO; sent to Camp Funston; he & 51 others refused to do any work connected with the military; …

operations.name: Louis Fraina

expected.charges: Anti-conscription activity (1917): conspiracy to obstruct the draft / Selective Service Act
expected.sentence: 30 days, served in 1919. (Separately indicted in the January 1920 CPA mass indictment for conspiracy to cause armed revolution, but abroad and never tried; ordered deported under the McCarran Act in 1952, but died in 1953 before removal.)

operations.source: https://www.marxists.org/history/usa/parties/spusa/1917/1005-nycall-frainaandcheneycases.pdf — transcription of New York Call October 5, 1917 page 5. Downloaded and rendered page 1 because text extraction had a broken character mapping. Explicit September 27 arrest with Ralph Cheney at the Labor Temple, and hearing before Judge Irvine (name as printed). Both were already out on $2,500 bail at publication; no uninterrupted September 1917–1919 custody inferred.

operations.name: Otto Frederick Schmidt

expected.name: Otto Frederick Schmidt
expected.description: Otto Frederick Schmidt was a twenty-six-year-old member of the IWW arrested in Spokane, Washington. Otto Frederick Schmidt was held for ten months in jail as a deportable alien. Originally detained at an immigration station, Schmidt was arrested without a warrant and held without benefit of a trial or hearing. Schmidt was denied letter-writing privileges and was forced to sleep on a " concrete floor" with "no bed." He fell ill at the immigration station and lost his " teeth and hair. " According to his cellmate, A. George Jensen, Schmidt "believed that the working class should organize to better their conditions. He was arrested for trying to make the world a fit place in which to live." Schmidt was transferred to the Walla Walla County Jail, where conditions remained very poor. When the IWW prisoners collectively protested their condition, the guards responded by hosing them down: A terrific stream of icy cold water was turned onto the sick, half-starved and helpless men, who were locked in a cage, trapped like so many rats. Men were lifted off their feet and battered against the steel bars by the force of the water. Within a few minutes mattresses and blankets were floating about the floor and five men were stretched out, bleeding and unconscious in the wreckage and water. Schmidt was one of the inmates found unconscious after the hosing, but he received no medical attention. His body was merely laid on a " bare iron bunk. " Later, when prison authorities decided he was sufficiently ill to require medical attention, Schmidt was transferred to the Spokane County Jail. But his condition continued to worsen: Schmidt was coughing; the froth was over his drawn lips. During his final days he was removed, sent to the Sacred Heart Hospital, where he died on December 2, 1918.

operations.source: https://depts.washington.edu/iww/map_killed.shtml — University of Washington IWW History Project explicitly identifies Otto Frederick Schmidt, December 2, 1918, Spokane, death while awaiting deportation. Corroborated by contemporary-cellmate account reproduced at https://weneverforget.org/tag/december-1918/ . Matches existing detailed biography. Record death and death in custody, not a fictitious release; initial admission remains unresolved.

operations.name: Carlos Steward

expected.sentence: 24 months imposed June 30, 2010 following a February 2010 guilty plea. Entered the federal prison camp in Montgomery, Alabama in August 2010. NWTRCC gives August 7, while a contemporary Nuclear Resister account describes reporting on Hiroshima Day (August 6); admission is retained at month precision pending resolution. December 1, 2011 marks transfer to a halfway house, not final federal release. The unsupported Edna Mahan women's prison association and exact-duration calculation are cleared.

operations.source: https://nwtrcc.org/resist/consequences/war-tax-resisters-taken-court/ — National War Tax Resistance Coordinating Committee court-history entry explicitly records Carlos Steward’s February 2010 guilty plea. Existing verdict, sentence, disputed August admission month, prison-to-halfway-house transfer and BOP endpoint preserved. No arrest day inferred from plea date.
